articles.title: Taiwan’s international enrolment up by 17% in 2025/26
articles.summary: Taiwan’s international student enrolment reached 140,420 in the 2025/26 academic year, marking a 17% increase from the previous year and setting a new all-time high. Of these students, approximately 90,000 are enrolled in degree programmes, while the remainder include exchange students, Mandarin-language learners, and students from China and Hong Kong.
articles.insight:
Taiwan’s 17% surge in international enrolment—especially the large cohort from China—may reflect shifting preferences among Asian students seeking alternatives to Western destinations, though it’s unclear whether this signals broader regional demand shifts or is driven by specific policy, pricing, or geopolitical factors.  
Admissions teams should monitor enrolment trends and visa processing times in key Asian markets, assess how Taiwan’s Mandarin-language offerings and degree affordability compare with their own value propositions, and review recruitment messaging for resonance with students prioritising language acquisition alongside academic credentials.

articles.title: Unions, advocacy groups sue to overturn US visa rule for foreign students, journalists
articles.summary: A coalition of unions and advocacy groups filed a lawsuit against the federal government on Tuesday to block a new U.S. visa rule that would restrict how long foreign students and journalists can stay in the country without applying for extensions. The plaintiffs seek to overturn the rule, which they argue imposes undue burdens on affected individuals and institutions.
articles.insight:
This news signals potential volatility in U.S. student visa policy, which may dampen demand from risk-averse applicants—especially in high-propensity markets like China and India—though actual enrollment impact depends on litigation outcomes and implementation timelines.  
Admissions teams should track the lawsuit’s progress, consult legal advisors on contingency planning for U.S. partner institutions, and assess whether messaging around visa stability needs updating in pre-application communications to affected source regions.

articles.title: Canada’s language training sector in “state of crisis” after further enrolment declines in 2025
articles.summary: Languages Canada’s 2025 Annual Survey Report states that the country’s language training sector is in a “state of crisis” due to further enrolment declines in 2025. The report is based on responses from over 150 Canadian English and French language programmes that participated in both the 2024 and 2025 surveys.
articles.insight:
Canada’s language training sector crisis may reflect broader shifts in international student preferences, potentially indicating reduced interest in Canada as a study destination due to visa processing delays, cost-of-living pressures, or evolving perceptions of post-study work opportunities—though direct spillover to other countries remains uncertain and context-dependent.  
Admissions teams should monitor application trends from key Canadian feeder markets (e.g., India, Nigeria, Philippines), track comparative visa policy changes, and assess whether language pathway partnerships with Canadian providers require contingency planning amid growing sector instability.

articles.title: Clare rejects Hanson’s “farce” claim as he defends international education reforms
articles.summary: Australia’s education minister Jason Clare rejected Pauline Hanson’s characterization of the country’s international education sector as a “farce.” Clare acknowledged that unscrupulous providers and substandard practices continue to threaten the sector’s reputation while defending ongoing reforms.
articles.insight:
Australia’s renewed focus on reforming its international education sector—amid political criticism of quality and integrity—may indirectly influence student demand, as perceptions of regulatory rigor and institutional reputation shift across key Asian source markets, though direct enrollment impacts remain uncertain without clearer policy outcomes.  
Admissions teams should monitor Australian government announcements on visa integrity measures, provider compliance enforcement, and scholarship expansions, while assessing whether competitor institutions in the UK, USA, or NZ are positioning themselves more prominently in response to perceived Australian volatility.

articles.title: How to help more of Hong Kong’s non-Chinese-speaking students reach university
articles.summary: The percentage of non-Chinese-speaking (NCS) students who sat the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) exams and were admitted to public universities has remained persistently low over the past five academic years. articles.insight:
This news suggests potential upward pressure on demand for English-medium undergraduate pathways among Hong Kong’s NCS students, though the extent depends on whether systemic barriers in local Chinese-language and maths requirements persist or worsen. It does not confirm a near-term exodus, but reflects structural friction that could gradually shift aspirational preferences toward overseas universities.  
Admissions teams should monitor DSE pass-rate trends for NCS cohorts—especially in Chinese and maths—and track any policy shifts in Hong Kong’s university admission criteria or language support provisions, as these may signal emerging cohort readiness or timing windows for targeted outreach.
